forces: Two violins, viola and two cellos
performers: Isaac Stern, Alexander Schneider, violins; Milton Katims, viola; Pablo Casals, Paul Tortelier, cellos
intro: Three inner voices sing while a violin and a plucked cello frame them: the Adagio of Schubert’s String Quintet begins with an extraordinary stillness. Pablo Casals and his Prades colleagues carry it through the violent F-minor middle section and its changed return.

sections.label: A · Three singing voices, one plucked cello
sections.mNote: Second violin, viola and first cello sustain the melody

sections.label: B · Violin and cello cry out in F minor
sections.mNote: Bowed bass and off-beat inner strings drive the duet

sections.label: A′ · E major, with a restless second cello
sections.mNote: The second cello adds running demisemiquavers beneath the returning melody

sections.label: Coda · F minor touches the final E major
sections.mNote: The middle section’s key returns in the last three bars

cues.title: A melody inside the quintet
cues.text: The second violin, viola and first cello sing a slow E-major melody. Around them, the first violin plays short, dotted phrases and the second cello plucks the bass. Five players seem to inhabit three different speeds.
cues.evidence: Schubert’s Werke, Series IV, No. 1 (Breitkopf & Härtel, 1890), Adagio opening; Misha Donat describes the inner melody, first-violin phrases and pizzicato bass in his 2012 note. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6016_67864
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A letter to Leipzig
cues.text: On 2 October 1828 Schubert writes to the publisher Heinrich Albert Probst with three piano sonatas, Heine songs and a new quintet to offer. The quintet is about to be tried out. He is thirty-one, and still looking for a publisher.
cues.evidence: Schubert to Probst, 2 October 1828, quoted in Misha Donat’s programme note; the work remains unpublished until 1853. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6016_67864

cues.title: F minor breaks in
cues.text: F minor arrives a semitone above E, fortissimo. The second cello takes up the bow, and the first violin and first cello launch a long melody together. The inner parts press against them with off-beat chords.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1890), Adagio middle section; Misha Donat describes the F-minor duet, syncopated inner accompaniment and active second cello. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6016_67864
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Violin and cello in octaves
cues.text: The first violin and first cello share the melody in octaves. Their wide separation makes one line sound almost orchestral, while the other cello drives beneath them. The two cellos now have utterly different jobs.
cues.evidence: Misha Donat’s programme note identifies violin and cello in octaves in the slow movement’s middle section and describes the second cello’s accompaniment. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6016_67864
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Twenty-two years of waiting
cues.text: The first known public performance comes in Vienna on 17 November 1850, twenty-two years after Schubert’s death. Publication follows in 1853. The manuscript and sketches are now lost.
cues.evidence: Composition and publication history, including première date and lost sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_Quintet_(Schubert).

cues.title: The cello cannot settle
cues.text: E major returns. The three inner players recover their broad melody, but the second cello now runs through demisemiquavers, exchanging flourishes with the first violin. The old stillness has quick notes moving around its edges.
cues.evidence: Misha Donat’s note describes the first-violin and second-cello dialogue around the unchanged inner melody. The demisemiquavers are identified in the Adagio account at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_Quintet_(Schubert); https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6016_67864.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: F minor touches the ending
cues.text: The last three bars briefly recover F minor, the key of the middle section, then return to E major. The disturbance is small enough to fit inside a farewell.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1890), Adagio, final three bars; harmonic close described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_Quintet_(Schubert).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Up a semitone, fortissimo
transitions.from: A · Three singing voices, one plucked cello
transitions.to: B · Violin and cello cry out in F minor
transitions.how: E major is interrupted by F minor, fortissimo. The second cello changes from plucked bass to bowed motion; first violin and first cello take the long melody in octaves, with syncopated chords between them.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1890), Adagio, p. 18; Misha Donat’s description of the middle section. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6016_67864

transitions.title: Broken chords find E major
transitions.from: B · Violin and cello cry out in F minor
transitions.to: A′ · E major, with a restless second cello
transitions.how: The F-minor passage subsides into quiet, separated chords. They lead back to E major and the sustained inner melody. First violin and second cello now exchange quick flourishes around the three other players.
transitions.evidence: Misha Donat’s programme note describes the faltering transition and varied reprise. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6016_67864

transitions.title: The F-minor chord returns
transitions.from: A′ · E major, with a restless second cello
transitions.to: Coda · F minor touches the final E major
transitions.how: In the last three bars, F minor briefly interrupts E major again. The five strings recover the home key at once and close softly.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1890), Adagio, final three bars on p. 25. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_Quintet_(Schubert)

source.title: Schubert, Streichquintett C-dur, Franz Schubert’s Werke, Serie IV No. 1 (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, 1890, plate F.S. 22)
source.locator: IMSLP #885759, second movement, Adagio, printed pages 17–25. The two cello parts are grouped together here. The last three bars appear above the Scherzo on page 25.

timeline.note: Second violin, viola and first cello sustain the melody between dotted first-violin phrases and plucked second cello.
First violin and first cello sing in octaves, fortissimo in F minor; the second cello drives beneath them.
The five strings retreat into quiet, separated chords on the way back to E major.
The inner melody returns in E major, surrounded by first-violin flourishes and running second-cello demisemiquavers.
A brief F-minor chord gives way to the E-major ending.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Isaac Stern (violin), Alexander Schneider (violin), Milton Katims (viola), Pablo Casals (cello), Paul Tortelier (cello)
fields.note: The Internet Archive item lists these five performers as creators; the Substack essay assigns the roles and calls the recording a Columbia release made at the Prades Festival. Which cellist plays the first cello part and which the second is not stated in any source consulted.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The performing edition is not identified. The Internet Archive file names print the posthumous opus number 163 for the work, which Schubert’s catalogue gives as D. 956.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.value: 1952 (the Casals Festival at Prades); one secondary source says July
fields.note: The LP sleeve notes say the recordings were made in Prades during the Casals Festival of 1952; the Discogs master release and a 6moons review also say 1952. Only the Substack essay by John Buxton gives a month, July 1952, so the month is not treated as established, and the day is not stated.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Prades, France (Prades Festival); the venue within Prades is not identified
fields.note: The sleeve notes say the recordings were made in Prades during the Casals Festival of 1952. Substack says the recording was made in Prades, France during the Prades Festival; Discogs and 6moons say it was recorded at the Prades Festival in 1952.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The label is the item’s publisher metadata and the title shown on its page.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: ML 4714 / SL-183, Casals Festival at Prades, Third Series
fields.note: The Internet Archive item page prints “Columbia Masterworks (ML 4714 / SL-183)” with publication date 1953. A 1976 CBS Classics reissue (61043) and a Philips issue (A 01188 L) are listed on Discogs and are not this carrier.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Side 1, second track of the LP (file 01.02 on the Internet Archive); matrix and take numbers are not established
fields.note: The Internet Archive file for the Adagio is a derivative linked to a segments file, so the cut between the first movement and the Adagio is the Internet Archive’s. No matrix or take numbers appear in the sources consulted.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Internet Archive LP digitisation: ripped by an Internet Archive associate at the Cebu scanning centre (rip station archivelp-rip-cebu04); the cover was scanned and the item created by another associate
fields.note: The item metadata names a ripping operator and a ripping scanner, a scanning centre (cebu) and a separate scanning operator. The item is listed in several vinyl collections, including the Boston Public Library’s; which physical copy was digitised is not stated.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.value: 4 January 2021 (the ripping date recorded in the item metadata)
fields.note: The metadata gives ripping_date 20210104123741. The artwork scan date and public date are 24 November 2020 and the added date is 4 January 2021; these are separate events and the scan and upload dates are not transfer dates.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Technics SL1200MK5 turntable with Audio-Technica AT95e cartridge, Radio Design Labs EZ-PH1 phono preamp and Focusrite Scarlett 2i2 interface; the Adagio file is an MP3 derivative of the side
fields.note: The hardware chain is the lineage field of the item metadata; the file inventory also reports generic SoX processing of the side files, with no settings. The equalisation curve, noise treatment, original recording engineering and playing-speed accuracy are not documented and are not inferred from the equipment names.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Schubert died in 1828. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about an unidentified modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: The Internet Archive item gives publication date 1953 and the Discogs master release gives the year 1953, so the 50-year European term expired before the 2013 extension. The item carries no licence statement; no US public-domain basis is claimed, and the 1953 date is not independently verified against a label image.
alts: Pre-1963 European public domain — territorial basis, publication 1953.
No licence or rights statement on the Internet Archive item.

composer.epithet: At seventeen he set a spinning wheel turning under Gretchen’s voice; at thirty-one he could make two cellos sing as if they had always belonged together.
facts: Vienna Stadtkonvikt, 1808–13; composition lessons with Antonio Salieri
School assistant; tutor to the Esterházy daughters at Zseliz in 1818 and 1824; independent composer
The singer Vogl, the poets Schober and Mayrhofer, the painter Schwind, Josef von Spaun
More than 600 songs; symphonies, chamber music, piano sonatas and duets, masses and stage works

quote.text: I like these songs more than all the others, and you will come to like them too.
quote.source: Schubert to his friends about Winterreise, 1827, as Josef von Spaun later recalled; our translation

composer.background:
In the Schubert family quartet, Franz played the viola. His brothers took the violins and his father the cello: the future songwriter learnt to make himself heard from an inner part. He was born on 31 January 1797 in Himmelpfortgrund, a Viennese suburb, and grew up in his father’s schoolhouse. His father taught him violin, his brother Ignaz piano, and the parish musician Michael Holzer helped with the rest. At eleven he entered the imperial chapel choir and the Stadtkonvikt boarding school, where the orchestra put Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven under his fingers.

Salieri began teaching him composition in 1812. The next year Schubert left the boarding school, trained as a teacher and returned to his father’s classroom as an assistant. On 19 October 1814, aged seventeen, he wrote Gretchen am Spinnrade. The piano’s right hand turns the wheel, the left hand works the treadle, and Goethe’s girl cannot stop thinking about Faust. At the remembered kiss the mechanism stops. The following year brought roughly 140 songs, among them Erlkönig, as well as church music, a symphony and works for the stage.
